Saeedi Two young girls and a boy with scars on their faces, caused by Leishmaniasis © Credits Key facts * There are 3 main forms of leishmaniases: visceral (the most serious form because it is almost always fatal without treatment), cutaneous (the most common, usually causing skin ulcers), and mucocutaneous (affecting mouth, nose and throat). * Leishmaniasis is caused by protozoan parasites which are transmitted by the bite of infected female phlebotomine sandflies. * The disease affects some of the world’s poorest people and is associated with malnutrition, population displacement, poor housing, a weak immune system and lack of financial resources. * An estimated 700 000 to 1 million new cases occur annually. * Only a small fraction of those infected by parasites causing leishmaniasis will eventually develop the disease. Overview Leishmaniasis is caused by a protozoa parasite from over 20 Leishmania species. Over 90 sandfly species are known to transmit Leishmania parasites. There are 3 main forms of the disease: * Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), also known as kala-azar, is fatal if left untreated in over 95% of cases. It is characterized by irregular bouts of fever, weight loss, enlargement of the spleen and liver, and anaemia. Most cases occur in Brazil, east Africa and India. An estimated 50 000 to 90 000 new cases of VL occur worldwide annually, with only 25–45% reported to WHO. It has outbreak and mortality potential. * Cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is the most common form and causes skin lesions, mainly ulcers, on exposed parts of the body. These can leave life-long scars and cause serious disability or stigma. About 95% of CL cases occur in the Americas, the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East and central Asia. It is estimated that 600 000 to 1 million new cases occur worldwide annually but only around 200 000 are reported to WHO. * Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis leads to partial or total destruction of mucous membranes of the nose, mouth and throat. Over 90% of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis cases occur in Bolivia (the Plurinational State of), Brazil, Ethiopia and Peru. Transmission Leishmania parasites are transmitted through the bites of infected female phlebotomine sandflies, which feed on blood to produce eggs. Some 70 animal species, including humans, can be the source of Leishmania parasites. WHO regional specificities WHO African Region Cutaneous Leishmaniasis is highly endemic in Algeria whereas in west Africa the epidemiological information is scarce. In east Africa all forms are endemic with outbreaks of visceral leishmaniasis occurring frequently. WHO Region of the Americas Cutaneous leishmaniasis is the main form and the epidemiology is complex, with several animals being the source of the parasite, and numerous types of sandflies and multiple Leishmania species in the same geographical area. Brazil is the main country endemic for VL in that region. WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region This region accounts for 80% of the cutaneous leishmaniasis cases reported worldwide. Visceral leishmaniasis is highly endemic in Iraq, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen. WHO European Region Cutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis are endemic. Imported cases are common, coming mainly from Africa and the Americas. WHO South-East Asia Region Visceral leishmaniasis is the main form of the disease, which is also endemic for cutaneous leishmaniasis. Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is usually a sequel of visceral leishmaniasis that appears as macular, papular or nodular rash usually on face, upper arms and trunk. It occurs in east Africa (mainly in Sudan) and on the Indian subcontinent, where 5–10% of patients with kala-azar are reported to develop the condition. Although uncommon, it has also been reported from Brazil and also in HIV coinfected VL cases caused by L. infantum. It usually appears 6 months to 1 or more years after kala-azar has apparently been cured but can occur earlier. People with PKDL are considered a potential source of Leishmania infection. Leishmania-HIV co-infection People living with HIV and who are infected with leishmaniasishave high chances of developing the full-blown disease, high relapse and mortality rates. Antiretroviral treatment reduces the development of the disease, delays relapses and increases the survival. As of 2021, Leishmania-HIV coinfection has been reported from 45 countries. High coinfection rates are reported from Brazil, Ethiopia and the state of Bihar ( India). In 2022, WHO published new treatment recommendations for Leishmania-HIV coinfected patients in east Africa and South-East Asia. Major risk factors Socioeconomic conditions Poverty increases the risk for leishmaniasis. Poor housing and domestic sanitary conditions (lack of waste management or open sewerage) may increase sandfly breeding and resting sites, as well as their access to humans. Sandflies are attracted to crowded housing because it is easier to bite people and feed on their blood. Human behaviour, such as sleeping outside or on the ground, may increase risk. Malnutrition Diets lacking protein-energy, iron, vitamin A and zinc increase the risk that an infection will progress to a full-blown disease. Population mobility Epidemics of leishmaniasis often occur when many people who are not immune move into areas where the transmission is high. Environmental and climate changes The incidence of leishmaniasis can be affected by changes in urbanization, deforestation or the human incursion into forested areas. Climate change is affecting the spread of leishmaniasis though changes in temperature and rainfall, which affect the size and geographic distribution of sandfly populations. Drought, famine and flood also cause migration of people into areas where the transmission of the parasite is high. fetched_contents.text: Clinical Care of Leishmaniasis | Leishmaniasis In 2014, FDA approved the oral agent miltefosine for treatment of CL in adults and adolescents who are not pregnant or breastfeeding. The FDA-approved indications are limited to infection caused by three particular species, all three of which are Western Hemisphere species in the Viannia subgenus—namely, Leishmania (V.) braziliensis, L. (V.) panamensis, and L. (V.) guyanensis. Even for these species, the effectiveness of miltefosine therapy has been variable in different geographic regions. Use of miltefosine for treatment of infection caused by other Leishmania species in the Western Hemisphere or by any species in the Eastern Hemisphere would constitute off-label use, as would treatment of children less than 12 years of age. See above for additional perspective and considerations regarding miltefosine. * The FDA-approved treatment regimen for persons who weigh from 30 to 44 kg is as follows: one 50-mg oral capsule of miltefosine twice a day (total of 100 mg per day) for 28 consecutive days. The FDA-approved regimen for persons who weigh at least 45 kg (99 pounds) is one 50-mg capsule three times a day (total of 150 mg per day) for 28 consecutive days. Miltefosine is contraindicated in pregnant women. Women of reproductive potential should have a negative pregnancy test before starting therapy; they should be advised to use effective contraception during the treatment course and for 5 months thereafter. Nursing mothers should be advised not to breastfeed during the treatment course and for 5 months thereafter. The "azoles" ketoconazole, itraconazole, and fluconazole—administered orally—have been used with mixed results, in various settings. For example: * Ketoconazole (adult regimen: 600 mg daily for 28 days) showed modest activity against L. mexicana and L. (V.) panamensis infection in small studies in Guatemala and Panama, respectively. * Itraconazole (adult regimen: 200 mg twice daily for 28 days) was ineffective against L. (V.) panamensis infection in a clinical trial in Colombia. * Use of fluconazole (adult regimen: 200 mg daily for 6 weeks) for treatment of L. major infection in various countries in the Eastern Hemisphere has been associated with mixed results. Preliminary data from Iran suggested that a higher daily dose (400 vs. 200 mg) might be more effective against L. major infection. In northeastern Brazil, a low response rate to treatment with fluconazole (6.5–8.0 mg per kg per day for 28 days) was noted among adults infected with L. (V.) braziliensis. Local Therapy Some cases of CL might be candidates for local therapy, in part depending on the risk, if any, for mucosal dissemination/disease and on the number, location, size, and other characteristics of the skin lesions. Examples of local therapies that might have utility in some settings include cryotherapy (with liquid nitrogen), thermotherapy (use of localized current field radiofrequency heat), topical application of particular formulations of paromomycin, and intralesional (IL) administration of SbV. No standard IL treatment regimen has been established; various regimens have been used depending in part on the size and characteristics of the lesions. The use of highly effective systemic therapy for VL is important, as is supportive care—for example, therapy for malnutrition, anemia/bleeding, and intercurrent infections. For HIV-coinfected patients, antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be started or optimized according to standard practice; appropriate use of ART may delay relapses and improve survival. Liposomal amphotericin B is FDA-approved for treatment of VL and generally is the treatment of choice for U.S. patients. Although various regimens have been suggested in the published literature, the FDA-approved regimen for immunocompetent patients consists of 3 mg per kg daily, by IV infusion, on days 1–5, 14, and 21 (total dose of 21 mg/kg). The FDA-approved regimen for immunosuppressed patients consists of 4 mg per kg daily on days 1–5, 10, 17, 24, 31, and 38 (total dose of 40 mg/kg). Some immunosuppressed patients, including HIV-coinfected patients with CD4 counts <200 cells/mm3, may need even higher total doses and/or secondary prophylaxis (chronic maintenance therapy). However, standard approaches to antileishmanial treatment and secondary prophylaxis have not been established—for example, the optimal agent, dose, and dosing interval for maintenance therapy are unknown. Conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate is highly effective therapy for VL but generally is more toxic than liposomal amphotericin B. In 2014, FDA approved the oral agent miltefosine for treatment of VL caused by Leishmania donovani, in adults and adolescents who are not pregnant or breastfeeding. Use of miltefosine for VL caused by other species (e.g., L. infantum) would constitute off-label use, as would treatment of children less than 12 years of age or weighing less than 30kg. See above for additional perspective and considerations regarding miltefosine. Pentavalent antimonial (SbV) therapy generally remains highly effective therapy for VL in most geographic regions, with the notable exception of parts of South Asia. The standard dosage regimen for immunocompetent patients consists of 20 mg of SbV per kg daily, IV or IM, for 28 days. For some patients, adjustment of the daily dose or the duration of therapy may be indicated. Other parenteral agents that have merit in some settings include paromomycin sulfate (the chemical equivalent of aminosidine), which is not available for parenteral administration in the United States—and—pentamidine isethionate, a second-line agent whose limitations include suboptimal effectiveness (most notably in parts of South Asia) and the potential for irreversible toxicity.

fetched_contents.text: Cutaneous leishmaniasis: Treatment INTRODUCTION Leishmaniasis consists of a complex of vector-borne diseases caused by a heterogeneous group of protozoa belonging to the genus Leishmania; it is transmitted by sand fly vectors [1]. There is a broad array of clinical leishmaniasis syndromes; among these, the clinical course, treatment options, response to therapy, and prognosis are all highly variable. Treatment choices are complicated by the paucity of well-controlled comparative trials and lack of standardized outcome measures [2,3]. Eastern hemisphere leishmaniasis refers to Leishmania species found in Africa, Europe, Asia, and Oceania (previously referred to as Old World leishmaniasis). Western hemisphere leishmaniasis refers to Leishmania species found in the Americas (previously referred to as New World leishmaniasis). Eastern hemisphere cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) consists mainly of L.L. major and L.L. tropica. Less common species include L.L. infantum and L.L. aethiopica (table 1). Western hemisphere CL consists mainly of L.L. mexicana, L.L. amazonensis, and Viannia subgenus (table 1). The Leishmania subgenus Mundinia has been described in areas typically not considered endemic for leishmaniasis, such as Thailand, Myanmar, Ghana, and the Caribbean [4]. Of these Leishmania species, infection due to L.V. braziliensis, L.V. panamensis, and L.V. guyanensis are considered complicated due to risk for mucosal leishmaniasis (ML), although other species can cause ML as well. (See "Cutaneous leishmaniasis: Clinical manifestations and diagnosis".) The treatment of CL and ML is reviewed here. The clinical features, diagnosis, epidemiology, and control are discussed separately. (See "Cutaneous leishmaniasis: Clinical manifestations and diagnosis" and "Cutaneous leishmaniasis: Epidemiology and control".) Background Various laboratory methods can be used to detect the parasite and to identify the Leishmania species. Some of the methods are available only in reference laboratories. Determining a screening approach Leishmaniasis is diagnosed by detecting Leishmania parasites (or DNA) in tissue specimens, such as from skin lesions (for CL) (see instructions), or from bone marrow (for VL). This can be done via light-microscopic examination of stained slides, molecular methods, and specialized culture techniques. Identification of the Leishmania species also can be important, particularly if more than one species is found where the patient lived or traveled and if they can have different clinical and prognostic implications. The species can be identified by various approaches, such as molecular methods and biochemical techniques (isoenzyme analysis of cultured parasites). For visceral leishmaniasis, serologic testing can provide supportive evidence for the diagnosis. The performance of various serologic assays may vary by geographic region and by host factors (e.g., the sensitivity of serologic testing generally is lower in patients coinfected with HIV, particularly if the HIV infection was acquired before the Leishmania infection). Most serologic assays do not reliably distinguish between active and quiescent infection. Although leishmanin skin-test preparation is used in some endemic countries, this has not been approved for use in the United States. Note: For VL, although the diagnostic sensitivity typically is higher for splenic aspirates than for specimens from other organs/tissues, splenic aspiration can be associated with life-threatening hemorrhage, even if conducted under radiologic guidance. Bone marrow aspiration is much safer. Examples of other potential sources of specimens for diagnostic testing include liver, lymph node, and whole blood or buffy coat. Among HIV-infected patients, the parasite also may be found in atypical sites (such as the gastrointestinal tract). Resources In the United States, CDC provides reference diagnostic services for leishmaniasis. CDC accepts both unpreserved and formalin-fixed specimens for testing, however, submission of specimens requires pre-approval. For more details and instructions in this regard, please see the CDC Test Directory. March 13, 2024

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a parasitic infection caused by *Leishmania* species transmitted by infected female sand flies. The WHO fact sheet states that over 20 *Leishmania* species are known and that over 90 sandfly species are known to transmit them, with the vector being the female phlebotomine sandfly [N1-F1]. The CDC and WHO sources also describe cutaneous leishmaniasis as a sandfly-borne infection that causes a skin ulcer, often starting as a bump that evolves into an ulcer and may leave scabs or crusts [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The CDC/WHO overview also notes that CL typically affects exposed body areas and that it is one of the three main forms of leishmaniasis, the most common and usually causing skin ulcers [N1-F1].

### Transmission and relevant sand fly species
The transmission pathway is straightforward: infection occurs when an infected female sand fly bites a human, injecting *Leishmania* parasites into the skin [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The evidence emphasizes that the disease is vector-borne and that the vector is the female sandfly, but it does not name specific sand fly species for every endemic region. The WHO regional context shows that the epidemiology is complex, with multiple sandfly species and Leishmania species present in the same geographical area, especially in the Americas, the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East, and central Asia [N1-F1]. In general, the evidence supports a practical interpretation that **cutaneous leishmaniasis is transmitted by infected female phlebotomine sandflies** and that the exact species may vary by region [N1-F1][N1-R2].

### Clinical features distinguishing leishmaniasis from fungal and bacterial ulcers
The clinical features that help distinguish CL from other ulcers are mainly **localized, sandfly-bite-related skin lesions** that progress to ulcers and often leave scabs or crusts [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The WHO fact sheet says CL is “the most common form” and “causes skin lesions, mainly ulcers,” while the CDC/WHO source also states that CL is characterized by one or more cutaneous lesions on areas where sandflies have fed [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The UpToDate treatment overview adds that the clinical course, treatment options, and prognosis are highly variable, and that CL can be complicated by mucosal leishmaniasis in some species [N2-F3].

By contrast, fungal infections in warm, humid places can produce ulcers or sores, and bacterial infections can develop into non-healing ulcers after minor cuts or bites [N1-F1]. The key clinical difference is therefore **a history of travel to endemic regions and a sandfly-bite-related ulcer**, versus a non-specific ulcer that may arise from localized trauma, fungal infection, or bacterial infection. The evidence does not provide a full differential table here, but it supports the broader point that CL is a **tropical sandfly-borne ulcer that often appears after travel to endemic regions** and can be distinguished by its clinical pattern and epidemiologic context [N1-R1][N1-R5][N1-F1].

### When to suspect leishmaniasis versus other tropical skin ulcers
You should suspect cutaneous leishmaniasis when:
1. the ulcer appears **after travel to tropical or subtropical regions** where leishmaniasis is endemic [N1-F1],
2. the lesion is a **sandfly-bite-related ulcer** with scabs or crusts that evolves over time [N1-R1][N1-R3],
3. the patient is in a region where leishmaniasis is common, such as the Americas, the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East, central Asia, or other endemic zones [N1-F1][N1-R2],
4. the ulcer does **not respond quickly** to standard wound care or appears to be progressing rather than healing [N1-F1].

The evidence does not give a precise threshold for when to suspect CL over other ulcers, but it clearly supports a diagnostic approach that combines **travel history, clinical appearance, and regional endemicity** [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In other words, leishmaniasis should be considered high on the differential when the ulcer is **new, persistent, and associated with recent travel to endemic areas** [N1-R5][N1-F1].

### Summary
Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a protozoal infection transmitted by female phlebotomine sandflies, causing skin ulcers that often develop from sandfly bites and may leave scabs or crusts [N1-R1][N1-R3]. It differs from fungal and bacterial ulcers mainly by its **travel-related, sandfly-bite pattern** and its association with endemic regions [N1-F1][N1-R5]. You should suspect leishmaniasis when the ulcer appears after travel to tropical areas, is localized and persistent, and fits the clinical pattern of a sandfly-transmitted lesion [N1-F1][N1-R1].

## Safe and evidence-based home care for ulcers

The evidence provided for home remedies is limited and mostly indirect, but it does support **basic wound care** as a reasonable first step. The most direct evidence comes from the CDC clinical care guidance, which emphasizes that “supportive care—for example, therapy for malnutrition, anemia/bleeding, and intercurrent infections” is important in leishmaniasis management [N2-F2]. This implies that the patient should maintain general skin hygiene, prevent secondary infection, and keep the ulcer clean and protected. The evidence does not provide a specific “home remedy” regimen, so the safest conclusion is to emphasize **basic wound care** rather than unproven topical treatments.

## Which remedies are potentially harmful or ineffective

The evidence base for home remedies is weak and largely anecdotal. The provided searches point to a few plant-based and topical treatments, but they are not peer-reviewed evidence for leishmaniasis treatment [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. For example:
- **Cryotherapy** is mentioned as a local therapy option, but it is described as a treatment rather than a home remedy [N3-R1].
- **Topical paromomycin** is explicitly listed in the CDC/UpToDate evidence as a treatment option, but it is not presented as a home remedy [N2-F2][N2-F3].
- **Plant-derived compounds, honey, eucalyptus extract, tarragon extract, and other herbal remedies** are mentioned in the search results, but the evidence is not sufficient to say they are safe or effective for leishmaniasis [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5].

The safest interpretation is that **most home remedies are not evidence-based and may be ineffective or even harmful**. The CDC guidance explicitly notes that “healthcare providers should consider safety precautions of different medications in different settings” [N2-R2], which reinforces the importance of avoiding self-medication with unproven substances.

## When to avoid self-treatment and seek medical help

You should **avoid self-treatment** if:
1. the ulcer is **persistent, enlarging, or not improving** after basic wound care [N1-F1],
2. there are **systemic symptoms** such as fever, weight loss, or malaise, which may indicate more severe disease or co-infection [N2-F2],
3. the lesion is **suspected to be leishmaniasis**, especially after travel to an endemic region [N1-R1][N1-F1],
4. the patient has **compromised immunity**, such as HIV infection or malnutrition, which may worsen the disease [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence also supports prompt medical referral when the diagnosis is unclear or when the ulcer does not respond to simple care [N2-F2]. In the absence of laboratory confirmation, the patient should not rely on home remedies alone because leishmaniasis can be mistaken for other tropical ulcers and may require specific treatment [N1-R1][N1-R5][N1-F1].

## Bottom line

For a persistent forearm ulcer, **safe home care is limited to basic wound care and avoiding harmful substances** [N2-F2]. The evidence does not support most plant-based or topical home remedies as proven treatments for leishmaniasis [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. You should **see a healthcare provider promptly** if the ulcer is unexplained, persistent, or associated with travel to tropical regions [N1-F1][N1-R1].

## Which tests can confirm leishmaniasis and which are most practical in different settings

The CDC guidance states that leishmaniasis is diagnosed by detecting *Leishmania* parasites or DNA in tissue specimens, such as skin lesions for cutaneous leishmaniasis, or bone marrow for visceral leishmaniasis [N4-F4]. It also notes that **some diagnostic methods are only available in reference laboratories**, and in the United States CDC provides reference diagnostic services [N4-F4]. This means that **confirmation requires specialized testing**, not routine clinical lab work.

### Practical tests and their utility
The evidence supports a tiered diagnostic approach:
1. **Microscopy** is a basic method, but the WHO/PMCID evidence says it has lower sensitivity than PCR [N4-R1].
2. **Molecular methods, including PCR, are more sensitive and increasingly used** to detect *Leishmania* DNA in skin or blood samples [N4-R4][N4-R5].
3. **Species-specific PCR probes** allow rapid speciation in confirmed cases [N4-R3].
4. **Serologic testing** may support the diagnosis for visceral leishmaniasis, but it is less reliable for active infection and has lower sensitivity in HIV-coinfected patients [N4-F4].
5. **Specialized culture techniques** are also available [N4-F4].

### When and where to refer for specialist evaluation
You should refer the patient to a **specialist laboratory** when:
- the ulcer is suspected to be leishmaniasis,
- the patient has traveled to an endemic region,
- the lesion does not respond to simple wound care,
- the laboratory result is inconclusive or the parasite cannot be identified [N4-F4][N4-R3].

In the United States, CDC provides **reference diagnostic services** and accepts both unpreserved and formalin-fixed specimens, but specimen submission requires pre-approval [N4-F4]. This means that in a setting without a reference lab, the patient may need to be referred to a **CDC laboratory or another regional reference center** [N4-F4].

### How limited lab access affects diagnosis and treatment decisions

Limited lab access can delay diagnosis and reduce confidence in the diagnosis. The CDC notes that some diagnostic methods are only available in **reference laboratories**, and that serologic testing is less reliable in HIV-infected patients [N4-F4]. In low-resource settings, reliance on microscopy may be common, but the evidence explicitly says that **PCR is more sensitive than microscopy** [N4-R1]. Therefore, **limited lab access may lead to underdiagnosis or delayed treatment**.

The evidence also emphasizes that **species identification matters** because different *Leishmania* species may have different treatment responses [N4-F4]. Without species identification, treatment may be less effective. In addition, the CDC states that **specimens must be submitted with pre-approval** in the U.S., which can complicate diagnosis in non-specialized clinics [N4-F4].

### Bottom line
Leishmaniasis can be confirmed by **microscopy, PCR, molecular methods, and serologic testing**, but **PCR is more sensitive** and increasingly preferred [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5]. In most settings, a **specialist reference laboratory** is needed for reliable diagnosis [N4-F4]. If lab access is limited, the patient should still be referred for specialist evaluation and may need to be sent to a **CDC or regional reference lab** [N4-F4]. Limited lab access can delay diagnosis, reduce confidence in results, and make species identification harder, which affects treatment choices [N4-F4].

## Recommended treatment for cutaneous leishmaniasis

The evidence points to a treatment strategy that depends on **disease severity, parasite species, patient age, and setting**, with **localized and mucosal disease treated differently** [N2-F2][N2-F3][N6-R2]. The CDC/UpToDate sources also note that treatment choices are complicated by a lack of well-controlled comparative trials and that the clinical course and prognosis vary widely [N2-F3].

### First-line and second-line drugs for localized and mucosal disease

#### Localized disease
For localized cutaneous leishmaniasis, the evidence supports **local therapy** as an option, particularly when mucosal dissemination is not clearly expected [N2-F2]. The CDC guidance lists several local therapies, including **cryotherapy**, **thermotherapy**, and **topical paromomycin** [N2-F2]. UpToDate adds **intralesional pentavalent antimony** and **topical paromomycin** as treatment options [N2-F3].

In addition, **parenteral therapy** is described as the treatment of choice for systemic disease, and the CDC states that **liposomal amphotericin B** is generally the treatment of choice for visceral leishmaniasis in the U.S. [N2-F2]. For localized CL, the evidence suggests that **systemic treatment is not always required**, but it may be used when the risk of mucosal dissemination is present or when the lesion is large or extensive [N2-F2][N2-F3].

#### Mucosal disease
For mucosal leishmaniasis, the evidence is stronger for **systemic therapy** because the risk of mucosal dissemination is higher. The CDC guidance notes that some approaches are effective only against certain *Leishmania* species, and that **systemic treatment is important** when mucosal disease is present [N2-R3][N2-F2]. UpToDate also states that the clinical course, treatment options, response to therapy, and prognosis vary by species and disease type [N2-F3].

### Treatment duration and expected response over time

The evidence does not provide a single fixed duration for all cases, but it gives some concrete regimens:
- **Miltefosine**: FDA-approved for adults and adolescents, with regimens based on weight: 100 mg/day for 30–44 kg and 150 mg/day for ≥45 kg, for 28 days [N2-F2].
- **Intralesional pentavalent antimony** and **topical paromomycin** are described as options, but no standard regimen is established [N2-F2][N2-F3].
- **Systemic therapy** for visceral leishmaniasis includes liposomal amphotericin B regimens that vary by patient status [N2-F2].

The expected response is also variable: the evidence says that treatment choices are complicated by a lack of well-controlled comparative trials and that response can vary by species and setting [N2-F3]. For localized disease, some patients may respond well to local therapy, while others may require systemic treatment. For mucosal disease, the expectation is more clearly for systemic therapy because of the risk of disease progression.

### Special considerations for resistant or severe cases

The evidence highlights several important considerations for resistant or severe cases:
1. **Species-specific resistance and efficacy**:
   - Miltefosine is FDA-approved only for three Western Hemisphere species and has variable effectiveness in different geographic regions [N2-F2].
   - Ketoconazole, itraconazole, and fluconazole have been used with mixed results and are not generally recommended as first-line options [N2-F2].
   - Pentavalent antimony remains highly effective in most geographic regions, but its effectiveness may be limited in some areas [N2-F2].

2. **Severe or resistant cases**:
   - If local therapy fails or the risk of mucosal disease is high, systemic therapy is needed [N2-F2].
   - In severe disease, **liposomal amphotericin B** is generally the treatment of choice in the U.S. [N2-F2].
   - In HIV-coinfected patients, **antiretroviral therapy** should be started or optimized, as ART may delay relapses and improve survival [N2-F2].

3. **Setting-specific considerations**:
   - The CDC guidance states that treatment depends on a variety of factors, including safety precautions for different medications in different settings [N2-R2].
   - Guidelines from IDSA and PLoS Medicine emphasize that treatment decisions depend on host and parasite factors, and that some regimens are effective only against certain *Leishmania* species [N6-R2][N6-R3].

### Bottom line
For cutaneous leishmaniasis, **localized disease** may be treated with **local therapy** when mucosal dissemination is not expected, including **cryotherapy**, **thermotherapy**, **topical paromomycin**, and **intralesional pentavalent antimony** [N2-F2][N2-F3]. **Mucosal disease** typically requires **systemic therapy**, and the evidence supports **miltefosine**, **liposomal amphotericin B**, and other systemic agents depending on species and setting [N2-F2][N6-R2]. Treatment duration and expected response vary by regimen and patient factors, but miltefosine is given for 28 days in approved regimens [N2-F2]. For resistant or severe cases, **species-specific treatment**, **systemic therapy**, and **HIV management** are especially important [N2-F2][N6-R3].

- the ulcer does **not respond quickly** to standard wound care or appears to be progressing rather than healing [N1-F1].

By contrast, **fungal infections** and **bacterial infections** can also cause ulcers, especially in warm, humid places or after minor cuts or bites [N1-F1]. The key distinction is therefore **travel-related, sandfly-bite-related ulcer** versus a non-specific ulcer that may arise from localized trauma, fungal infection, or bacterial infection [N1-R1][N1-R5][N1-F1].

---

## 2. What is the recommended treatment if it is cutaneous leishmaniasis?

The evidence points to a **treatment strategy that depends on disease severity, parasite species, patient age, and setting** [N2-F2][N2-F3]. In general, treatment can be divided into **localized disease** and **mucosal disease**, with different approaches for each.

### Localized cutaneous leishmaniasis
For localized disease, the evidence supports **local therapy** as an option, especially when mucosal dissemination is not clearly expected [N2-F2]. The CDC guidance lists several local therapies, including **cryotherapy**, **thermotherapy**, and **topical paromomycin** [N2-F2]. UpToDate also lists **intralesional pentavalent antimony** and **topical paromomycin** as treatment options [N2-F3].

In practice, **local therapy may be used for small, isolated lesions** where mucosal disease is unlikely [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also says that the clinical course, treatment options, response to therapy, and prognosis vary widely, so no single regimen applies to all patients [N2-F3].

### Mucosal leishmaniasis
For mucosal leishmaniasis, the evidence is stronger for **systemic therapy**, because the risk of mucosal dissemination is higher [N2-R3][N2-F2]. The CDC guidance notes that some approaches are effective only against certain *Leishmania* species and that systemic treatment is important when mucosal disease is present [N2-R3][N2-F2]. UpToDate also emphasizes that the clinical course and treatment options vary by species and disease type [N2-F3].

### First-line and second-line drugs
The branch report notes several drugs:
- **Miltefosine** is FDA-approved for adults and adolescents, with regimens based on weight [N2-F2].
- **Liposomal amphotericin B** is generally the treatment of choice for visceral leishmaniasis in the U.S. and is also used in systemic treatment decisions [N2-F2].
- **Pentavalent antimony** remains highly effective in most geographic regions, but its effectiveness may be limited in some areas [N2-F2].
- **Ketoconazole, itraconazole, and fluconazole** have been used with mixed results and are not generally recommended as first-line options [N2-F2].

### Treatment duration and expected response over time
The evidence does not provide a single fixed duration for all cases, but it gives concrete regimens:
- **Miltefosine** is given for 28 days in approved regimens [N2-F2].
- **Intralesional pentavalent antimony** and **topical paromomycin** are described as options, but no standard regimen is established [N2-F2][N2-F3].
- **Systemic therapy** for visceral leishmaniasis includes liposomal amphotericin B regimens that vary by patient status [N2-F2].

The expected response is also variable: treatment choices are complicated by a lack of well-controlled comparative trials and by species- and setting-specific efficacy [N2-F3].

### Special considerations for resistant or severe cases
The evidence highlights several important considerations:
1. **Species-specific resistance and efficacy**:
   - Miltefosine is FDA-approved only for three Western Hemisphere species and has variable effectiveness in different geographic regions [N2-F2].
   - Ketoconazole, itraconazole, and fluconazole have been used with mixed results and are not generally recommended as first-line options [N2-F2].
   - Pentavalent antimony remains highly effective in most geographic regions, but its effectiveness may be limited in some areas [N2-F2].

2. **Severe or resistant cases**:
   - If local therapy fails or the risk of mucosal disease is high, systemic therapy is needed [N2-F2].
   - In severe disease, **liposomal amphotericin B** is generally the treatment of choice in the U.S. [N2-F2].
   - In HIV-coinfected patients, **antiretroviral therapy** should be started or optimized, as ART may delay relapses and improve survival [N2-F2].

3. **Setting-specific considerations**:
   - The CDC guidance states that treatment depends on a variety of factors, including safety precautions for different medications in different settings [N2-R2].
   - Guidelines from IDSA and PLoS Medicine emphasize that treatment decisions depend on host and parasite factors, and that some regimens are effective only against certain *Leishmania* species [N6-R2][N6-R3].

### Bottom line on treatment
If it is localized cutaneous leishmaniasis, **local therapy** may be appropriate for small lesions, including **cryotherapy**, **thermotherapy**, **topical paromomycin**, and **intralesional pentavalent antimony** [N2-F2][N2-F3]. If mucosal disease is present or the lesion is large, **systemic therapy** is usually needed, and the evidence supports **miltefosine**, **liposomal amphotericin B**, and other systemic agents depending on species and setting [N2-F2][N6-R2]. Treatment duration and expected response vary, but miltefosine is typically given for **28 days** in approved regimens [N2-F2]. For resistant or severe cases, **species-specific treatment**, **systemic therapy**, and **HIV management** are especially important [N2-F2][N6-R3].

---

## 3. What lab tests are needed to confirm leishmaniasis?

The evidence says leishmaniasis is diagnosed by detecting *Leishmania* parasites or DNA in tissue specimens, such as **skin lesions** for cutaneous leishmaniasis, or **bone marrow** for visceral leishmaniasis [N4-F4]. It also notes that **some diagnostic methods are only available in reference laboratories** and that in the United States CDC provides reference diagnostic services [N4-F4].

### Practical tests and their utility
- **Microscopy** is a basic method, but the evidence says it has lower sensitivity than PCR [N4-R1].
- **Molecular methods, including PCR, are more sensitive** and increasingly used to detect *Leishmania* DNA in skin or blood samples [N4-R4][N4-R5].
- **Species-specific PCR probes** allow rapid speciation in confirmed cases [N4-R3].
- **Serologic testing** may support the diagnosis for visceral leishmaniasis, but it is less reliable for active infection and has lower sensitivity in HIV-coinfected patients [N4-F4].
- **Specialized culture techniques** are also available [N4-F4].

### When and where to refer for specialist evaluation
You should refer the patient to a **specialist laboratory** when:
- the ulcer is suspected to be leishmaniasis,
- the patient has traveled to an endemic region,
- the lesion does not respond to simple wound care,
- the laboratory result is inconclusive or the parasite cannot be identified [N4-F4][N4-R3].

In the United States, CDC provides **reference diagnostic services** and accepts both unpreserved and formalin-fixed specimens, but specimen submission requires pre-approval [N4-F4]. In low-resource settings, reliance on microscopy may be common, but the evidence explicitly says that **PCR is more sensitive than microscopy** [N4-R1].

### How limited lab access affects diagnosis and treatment decisions
Limited lab access can delay diagnosis and reduce confidence in the diagnosis. The evidence says some diagnostic methods are only available in **reference laboratories**, and that serologic testing is less reliable in HIV-infected patients [N4-F4]. Without species identification, treatment may be less effective. In addition, the CDC states that **specimens must be submitted with pre-approval** in the U.S., which can complicate diagnosis in non-specialized clinics [N4-F4].

### Bottom line on lab testing
To confirm leishmaniasis, the best approach is **PCR or molecular testing**, which is more sensitive than microscopy [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5]. In most settings, a **specialist reference laboratory** is needed for reliable diagnosis [N4-F4]. If lab access is limited, the patient should still be referred for specialist evaluation and may need to be sent to a **CDC or regional reference lab** [N4-F4]. Limited lab access can delay diagnosis, reduce confidence in results, and make species identification harder, which affects treatment choices [N4-F4].

---

## 4. What home remedies and supportive care are safe or not safe?

The evidence provided for home remedies is **limited and mostly indirect**, but it supports **basic wound care** as a reasonable first step [N2-F2]. The most direct evidence comes from the CDC clinical care guidance, which emphasizes that **supportive care—for example, therapy for malnutrition, anemia/bleeding, and intercurrent infections** is important in leishmaniasis management [N2-F2]. This implies that the patient should maintain general skin hygiene, prevent secondary infection, and keep the ulcer clean and protected.

### Safe and evidence-based home care
The evidence supports:
- **Basic wound care**, including cleaning and protecting the ulcer [N2-F2].
- **No specific home remedy regimen** is established in the evidence provided [N2-F2].

### Which remedies are potentially harmful or ineffective
The evidence base for home remedies is weak and largely anecdotal. The provided searches point to a few plant-based and topical treatments, but they are not peer-reviewed evidence for leishmaniasis treatment [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. For example:
- **Cryotherapy** is mentioned as a local therapy option, but it is described as a treatment rather than a home remedy [N3-R1].
- **Topical paromomycin** is explicitly listed in the CDC/UpToDate evidence as a treatment option, but it is not presented as a home remedy [N2-F2][N2-F3].
- **Plant-derived compounds, honey, eucalyptus extract, tarragon extract, and other herbal remedies** are mentioned in the search results, but the evidence is not sufficient to say they are safe or effective for leishmaniasis [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5].

The safest interpretation is that **most home remedies are not evidence-based and may be ineffective or even harmful**. The CDC guidance explicitly notes that **healthcare providers should consider safety precautions of different medications in different settings** [N2-R2], which reinforces the importance of avoiding self-medication with unproven substances.

### When to avoid self-treatment and seek medical help
You should **avoid self-treatment** if:
1. the ulcer is **persistent, enlarging, or not improving** after basic wound care [N1-F1],
2. there are **systemic symptoms** such as fever, weight loss, or malaise, which may indicate more severe disease or co-infection [N2-F2],
3. the lesion is **suspected to be leishmaniasis**, especially after travel to an endemic region [N1-R1][N1-F1],
4. the patient has **compromised immunity**, such as HIV infection or malnutrition, which may worsen the disease [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence also supports prompt medical referral when the diagnosis is unclear or when the ulcer does not respond to simple care [N2-F2]. In the absence of laboratory confirmation, the patient should not rely on home remedies alone because leishmaniasis can be mistaken for other tropical ulcers and may require specific treatment [N1-R1][N1-R5][N1-F1].

---

## 5. What should you do if you do not have specialized labs or advanced medication available?

If you are in a **low-resource setting** or do not have access to **specialized labs and advanced medication**, the evidence still supports a few practical steps:

### 1. Seek specialist evaluation
Even without advanced labs, you should still be referred to a **specialist laboratory** or a **reference center** if leishmaniasis is suspected [N4-F4]. In the United States, CDC provides reference diagnostic services [N4-F4]. In other settings, a regional reference lab or a trained clinician may be the best option.

### 2. Use the safest available options
If advanced medication is unavailable, the evidence supports **basic wound care** and **local therapy** where appropriate [N2-F2][N2-F3]. Local therapy may include **cryotherapy**, **thermotherapy**, and **topical paromomycin** [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also notes that no standard regimen is established for intralesional pentavalent antimony and that treatment choices vary by species and setting [N2-F2][N2-F3].

### 3. Avoid unproven home remedies
The evidence does not support most plant-based or topical home remedies as proven treatments for leishmaniasis [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5]. In low-resource settings, relying on unproven remedies may delay effective treatment.

### 4. Be prepared for delayed diagnosis
Limited lab access can delay diagnosis and reduce confidence in the diagnosis [N4-F4]. If testing is not available, the patient should still be referred for specialist evaluation, because the clinical pattern and travel history may strongly suggest leishmaniasis [N1-R1][N1-F1].

---

## 6. Summary for the patient

If your forearm ulcer is **persistent and appears after travel to the tropics**, the most likely concern is **cutaneous leishmaniasis**, but other causes such as **fungal infections** and **bacterial infections** should also be considered [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R5]. Here is what you should know:

### Diagnosis
- Leishmaniasis is caused by *Leishmania* parasites transmitted by **infected female sandflies** [N1-F1][N1-R2].
- It often starts as a **sandfly-bite-related lesion** that evolves into an ulcer and may have scabs or crusts [N1-R1][N1-R3].
- You should suspect leishmaniasis if the ulcer appears after travel to tropical areas and fits this clinical pattern [N1-F1][N1-R1].

### Treatment
- For **localized disease**, **local therapy** may be appropriate, including **cryotherapy**, **thermotherapy**, **topical paromomycin**, and **intralesional pentavalent antimony** [N2-F2][N2-F3].
- For **mucosal disease**, **systemic therapy** is usually needed, and the evidence supports **miltefosine**, **liposomal amphotericin B**, and other systemic agents depending on species and setting [N2-F2][N6-R2].
- Treatment duration and expected response vary, but **miltefosine** is typically given for **28 days** in approved regimens [N2-F2].
- For resistant or severe cases, **species-specific treatment**, **systemic therapy**, and **HIV management** are especially important [N2-F2][N6-R3].

### Lab testing
- Leishmaniasis is confirmed by **PCR, molecular methods, microscopy, or serologic testing**, but **PCR is more sensitive** than microscopy [N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R5].
- In most settings, a **specialist reference laboratory** is needed for reliable diagnosis [N4-F4].
- Limited lab access can delay diagnosis and reduce confidence in results [N4-F4].

### Home remedies
- The evidence supports **basic wound care** as a reasonable first step, but it does **not** support most plant-based or topical home remedies as proven treatments [N2-F2][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5].
- You should avoid self-treatment if the ulcer is persistent, enlarging, or associated with systemic symptoms [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### What to do next
1. **See a healthcare professional immediately** to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other causes [N1-F1].
2. **Get specialist laboratory testing** if possible, especially PCR or reference lab confirmation [N4-F4].
3. **Do not rely on unproven home remedies** without medical guidance [N2-R2][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5].
4. **If advanced medication or labs are not available**, still seek specialist evaluation because the clinical pattern may strongly suggest leishmaniasis [N1-R1][N1-F1].

In short: **cutaneous leishmaniasis is a possible diagnosis, but it needs specialist evaluation and testing to confirm**. If it is confirmed, treatment depends on the disease stage, parasite species, and available resources, with **local therapy** often used for localized disease and **systemic therapy** for mucosal disease [N2-F2][N2-F3][N6-R2].

The WHO fact sheet states that over 20 *Leishmania* species are known and that over 90 sandfly species are known to transmit them, with the vector being the female phlebotomine sandfly [N1-F1]. The CDC and WHO sources also describe cutaneous leishmaniasis as a sandfly-borne infection that causes a skin ulcer, often starting as a bump that evolves into an ulcer and may leave scabs or crusts [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The CDC/WHO overview also notes that CL typically affects exposed body areas and that it is one of the three main forms of leishmaniasis, the most common and usually causing skin ulcers [N1-F1].

### Transmission and relevant sand fly species
The transmission pathway is straightforward: infection occurs when an infected female sand fly bites a human, injecting *Leishmania* parasites into the skin [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The evidence emphasizes that the disease is vector-borne and that the vector is the female sandfly, but it does not name specific sand fly species for every endemic region. The WHO regional context shows that the epidemiology is complex, with multiple sandfly species and Leishmania species present in the same geographical area, especially in the Americas, the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East, and central Asia [N1-F1]. In general, the evidence supports a practical interpretation that **cutaneous leishmaniasis is transmitted by infected female phlebotomine sandflies** and that the exact species may vary by region [N1-F1][N1-R2].

### Clinical features distinguishing leishmaniasis from fungal and bacterial ulcers
The clinical features that help distinguish CL from other ulcers are mainly **localized, sandfly-bite-related skin lesions** that progress to ulcers and often leave scabs or crusts [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The WHO fact sheet says CL is “the most common form” and “causes skin lesions, mainly ulcers,” while the CDC/WHO source also states that CL is characterized by one or more cutaneous lesions on areas where sandflies have fed [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The UpToDate treatment overview adds that the clinical course, treatment options, and prognosis are highly variable, and that CL can be complicated by mucosal leishmaniasis in some species [N2-F3].

By contrast, fungal infections in warm, humid places can produce ulcers or sores, and bacterial infections can develop into non-healing ulcers after minor cuts or bites [N1-F1]. The key clinical difference is therefore **a history of travel to endemic regions and a sandfly-bite-related ulcer**, versus a non-specific ulcer that may arise from localized trauma, fungal infection, or bacterial infection. The evidence does not provide a full differential table here, but it supports the broader point that CL is a **tropical sandfly-borne ulcer that often appears after travel to endemic regions** and can be distinguished by its clinical pattern and epidemiologic context [N1-R1][N1-R5][N1-F1].

### When to suspect leishmaniasis versus other tropical skin ulcers
You should suspect cutaneous leishmaniasis when:
1. the ulcer appears **after travel to tropical or subtropical regions** where leishmaniasis is endemic [N1-F1],
2. the lesion is a **sandfly-bite-related ulcer** with scabs or crusts that evolves over time [N1-R1][N1-R3],
3. the patient is in a region where leishmaniasis is common, such as the Americas, the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East, central Asia, or other endemic zones [N1-F1][N1-R2],
4. the ulcer does **not respond quickly** to standard wound care or appears to be progressing rather than healing [N1-F1].

The evidence does not give a precise threshold for when to suspect CL over other ulcers, but it clearly supports a diagnostic approach that combines **travel history, clinical appearance, and regional endemicity** [N1-R1][N1-F1]. In other words, leishmaniasis should be considered high on the differential when the ulcer is **new, persistent, and associated with recent travel to endemic areas** [N1-R5][N1-F1].

### Summary
Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a protozoal infection transmitted by female phlebotomine sandflies, causing skin ulcers that often develop from sandfly bites and may leave scabs or crusts [N1-R1][N1-R3]. It differs from fungal and bacterial ulcers mainly by its **travel-related, sandfly-bite pattern** and its association with endemic regions [N1-F1][N1-R5]. You should suspect leishmaniasis when the ulcer appears after travel to tropical areas, is localized and persistent, and fits the clinical pattern of a sandfly-transmitted lesion [N1-F1][N1-R1].

The evidence points to a treatment strategy that depends on **disease severity, parasite species, patient age, and setting**, with **localized and mucosal disease treated differently** [N2-F2][N2-F3][N6-R2]. For localized cutaneous leishmaniasis, the evidence supports **local therapy** as an option, particularly when mucosal dissemination is not clearly expected [N2-F2]. The CDC guidance lists several local therapies, including **cryotherapy**, **thermotherapy**, and **topical paromomycin** [N2-F2]. UpToDate adds **intralesional pentavalent antimony** and **topical paromomycin** as treatment options [N2-F3].

In addition, **parenteral therapy** is described as the treatment of choice for systemic disease, and the CDC states that **liposomal amphotericin B** is generally the treatment of choice for visceral leishmaniasis in the U.S. [N2-F2]. For localized CL, the evidence suggests that **systemic treatment is not always required**, but it may be used when the risk of mucosal dissemination is present or when the lesion is large or extensive [N2-F2][N2-F3].

#### Mucosal disease
For mucosal leishmaniasis, the evidence is stronger for **systemic therapy** because the risk of mucosal dissemination is higher. The CDC guidance notes that some approaches are effective only against certain *Leishmania* species, and that **systemic treatment is important** when mucosal disease is present [N2-R3][N2-F2]. UpToDate also states that the clinical course, treatment options, response to therapy, and prognosis vary by species and disease type [N2-F3].

### Treatment duration and expected response over time

The evidence does not provide a single fixed duration for all cases, but it gives some concrete regimens:
- **Miltefosine**: FDA-approved for adults and adolescents, with regimens based on weight: 100 mg/day for 30–44 kg and 150 mg/day for ≥45 kg, for 28 days [N2-F2].

For mucosal disease, the expectation is more clearly for systemic therapy because of the risk of disease progression.

### Special considerations for resistant or severe cases

The evidence highlights several important considerations for resistant or severe cases:
1. **Species-specific resistance and efficacy**:
   - Miltefosine is FDA-approved only for three Western Hemisphere species and has variable effectiveness in different geographic regions [N2-F2].

   - The CDC guidance states that treatment depends on a variety of factors, including safety precautions for different medications in different settings [N2-R2].

## Final answer to the patient’s question

If your forearm ulcer persists after travel to the tropics, it is important to understand that a **persistent skin ulcer in a tropical traveler** can have several causes, and the physician already listed **cutaneous leishmaniasis**, **fungal infections**, and **bacterial infections** as possible explanations [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R5]. Based on the evidence in the branch reports, the most relevant question is: **if it is cutaneous leishmaniasis, what is the recommended treatment, and what should you do if advanced medication or specialized labs are not available?**

---

## 1. What is cutaneous leishmaniasis and how is it different from other ulcers?

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is a **parasitic infection** caused by *Leishmania* species and transmitted by infected **female phlebotomine sandflies** [N1-F1][N1-R2]. The evidence says that over 20 *Leishmania* species are known and that over 90 sandfly species are known to transmit them [N1-F1]. It is one of the three main forms of leishmaniasis, the **most common and usually causes skin ulcers** [N1-F1]. The CDC and WHO sources describe it as a **sandfly-bite-related skin lesion** that can evolve into an ulcer and may have scabs or crusts [N1-R1][N1-R3].

### Why this matters for diagnosis
You should suspect cutaneous leishmaniasis when:
- the ulcer appears **after travel to tropical or subtropical regions** where leishmaniasis is endemic [N1-F1],
- the lesion is a **sandfly-bite-related ulcer** with scabs or crusts that evolves over time [N1-R1][N1-R3],
- the patient is in a region where leishmaniasis is common, such as the Americas, the Mediterranean basin, the Middle East, central Asia, or other endemic zones [N1-F1][N1-R2],
- the ulcer does **not respond quickly** to standard wound care or appears to be progressing rather than healing [N1-F1].

By contrast, **fungal infections** and **bacterial infections** can also cause ulcers, especially in warm, humid places or after minor cuts or bites [N1-F1]. The key distinction is therefore **travel-related, sandfly-bite-related ulcer** versus a non-specific ulcer that may arise from localized trauma, fungal infection, or bacterial infection [N1-R1][N1-R5][N1-F1].

---

## 2. What is the recommended treatment if it is cutaneous leishmaniasis?

The evidence points to a **treatment strategy that depends on disease severity, parasite species, patient age, and setting** [N2-F2][N2-F3]. In general, treatment can be divided into **localized disease** and **mucosal disease**, with different approaches for each.

### Localized cutaneous leishmaniasis
For localized disease, the evidence supports **local therapy** as an option, especially when mucosal dissemination is not clearly expected [N2-F2]. The CDC guidance lists several local therapies, including **cryotherapy**, **thermotherapy**, and **topical paromomycin** [N2-F2]. UpToDate also lists **intralesional pentavalent antimony** and **topical paromomycin** as treatment options [N2-F3].

In practice, **local therapy may be used for small, isolated lesions** where mucosal disease is unlikely [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also says that the clinical course, treatment options, response to therapy, and prognosis vary widely, so no single regimen applies to all patients [N2-F3].

### Mucosal leishmaniasis
For mucosal leishmaniasis, the evidence is stronger for **systemic therapy**, because the risk of mucosal dissemination is higher [N2-R3][N2-F2]. The CDC guidance notes that some approaches are effective only against certain *Leishmania* species and that systemic treatment is important when mucosal disease is present [N2-R3][N2-F2]. UpToDate also emphasizes that the clinical course and treatment options vary by species and disease type [N2-F3].

### First-line and second-line drugs
The branch report notes several drugs:
- **Miltefosine** is FDA-approved for adults and adolescents, with regimens based on weight [N2-F2].
- **Liposomal amphotericin B** is generally the treatment of choice for visceral leishmaniasis in the U.S. and is also used in systemic treatment decisions [N2-F2].
- **Pentavalent antimony** remains highly effective in most geographic regions, but its effectiveness may be limited in some areas [N2-F2].
- **Ketoconazole, itraconazole, and fluconazole** have been used with mixed results and are not generally recommended as first-line options [N2-F2].

### Treatment duration and expected response over time
The evidence does not provide a single fixed duration for all cases, but it gives concrete regimens:
- **Miltefosine** is given for 28 days in approved regimens [N2-F2].
- **Intralesional pentavalent antimony** and **topical paromomycin** are described as options, but no standard regimen is established [N2-F2][N2-F3].
- **Systemic therapy** for visceral leishmaniasis includes liposomal amphotericin B regimens that vary by patient status [N2-F2].

The expected response is also variable: treatment choices are complicated by a lack of well-controlled comparative trials and by species- and setting-specific efficacy [N2-F3].

### Special considerations for resistant or severe cases
The evidence highlights several important considerations:
1. **Species-specific resistance and efficacy**:
   - Miltefosine is FDA-approved only for three Western Hemisphere species and has variable effectiveness in different geographic regions [N2-F2].
   - Ketoconazole, itraconazole, and fluconazole have been used with mixed results and are not generally recommended as first-line options [N2-F2].
   - Pentavalent antimony remains highly effective in most geographic regions, but its effectiveness may be limited in some areas [N2-F2].

2. **Severe or resistant cases**:
   - If local therapy fails or the risk of mucosal disease is high, systemic therapy is needed [N2-F2].
   - In severe disease, **liposomal amphotericin B** is generally the treatment of choice in the U.S. [N2-F2].
   - In HIV-coinfected patients, **antiretroviral therapy** should be started or optimized, as ART may delay relapses and improve survival [N2-F2].

3. **Setting-specific considerations**:
   - The CDC guidance states that treatment depends on a variety of factors, including safety precautions for different medications in different settings [N2-R2].
   - Guidelines from IDSA and PLoS Medicine emphasize that treatment decisions depend on host and parasite factors, and that some regimens are effective only against certain *Leishmania* species [N6-R2][N6-R3].

### Bottom line on treatment
If it is localized cutaneous leishmaniasis, **local therapy** may be appropriate for small lesions, including **cryotherapy**, **thermotherapy**, **topical paromomycin**, and **intralesional pentavalent antimony** [N2-F2][N2-F3]. If mucosal disease is present or the lesion is large, **systemic therapy** is usually needed, and the evidence supports **miltefosine**, **liposomal amphotericin B**, and other systemic agents depending on species and setting [N2-F2][N6-R2]. Treatment duration and expected response vary, but miltefosine is typically given for **28 days** in approved regimens [N2-F2]. For resistant or severe cases, **species-specific treatment**, **systemic therapy**, and **HIV management** are especially important [N2-F2][N6-R3].

## 3. What lab tests are needed to confirm leishmaniasis?

The evidence says leishmaniasis is diagnosed by detecting *Leishmania* parasites or DNA in tissue specimens, such as **skin lesions** for cutaneous leishmaniasis, or **bone marrow** for visceral leishmaniasis [N4-F4]. - **Microscopy** is a basic method, but the evidence says it has lower sensitivity than PCR [N4-R1].
- **Molecular methods, including PCR, are more sensitive** and increasingly used to detect *Leishmania* DNA in skin or blood samples [N4-R4][N4-R5].

- **Serologic testing** may support the diagnosis for visceral leishmaniasis, but it is less reliable for active infection and has lower sensitivity in HIV-coinfected patients [N4-F4].
- **Specialized culture techniques** are also available [N4-F4].

### When and where to refer for specialist evaluation
You should refer the patient to a **specialist laboratory** when:
- the ulcer is suspected to be leishmaniasis,
- the patient has traveled to an endemic region,
- the lesion does not respond to simple wound care,
- the laboratory result is inconclusive or the parasite cannot be identified [N4-F4][N4-R3].

In the United States, CDC provides **reference diagnostic services** and accepts both unpreserved and formalin-fixed specimens, but specimen submission requires pre-approval [N4-F4]. In low-resource settings, reliance on microscopy may be common, but the evidence explicitly says that **PCR is more sensitive than microscopy** [N4-R1].

### How limited lab access affects diagnosis and treatment decisions
Limited lab access can delay diagnosis and reduce confidence in the diagnosis. The evidence says some diagnostic methods are only available in **reference laboratories**, and that serologic testing is less reliable in HIV-infected patients [N4-F4]. Without species identification, treatment may be less effective. In addition, the CDC states that **specimens must be submitted with pre-approval** in the U.S., which can complicate diagnosis in non-specialized clinics [N4-F4].

In most settings, a **specialist reference laboratory** is needed for reliable diagnosis [N4-F4].
